name: Pyruvic acid peel

lead: Pyruvic acid peels are superficial chemical peels applied in a clinic, mostly studied for acne.
The published evidence is thin: a small 2014 comparison with salicylic acid peels in 20 acne patients is the main study found.

paras: Pyruvic acid is a keratolytic alpha-keto acid that loosens the outer skin layers so they shed, which is how peels are described to work.
Peels in general can cause redness, photosensitivity, pigment change and, rarely, scarring. Pyruvic acid peels are applied by clinicians.

lead: A pyruvic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel that uses pyruvic acid, an alpha-keto acid, applied to the skin by a clinician to loosen and shed the outer layers. It is described in dermatology literature as a keratolytic peel used mainly in acne vulgaris.[1]

Published evidence is small. One comparison of 50% pyruvic acid and 30% salicylic acid peels in 20 patients with acne measured effects on facial sebum secretion.[1] Chemical peels in general are described as causing a controlled injury that makes the skin peel, with risks including prolonged redness, pigment change and scarring.[2]

paras: Pyruvic acid is grouped with the superficial peeling agents, alongside alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic acid and beta hydroxy acids such as salicylic acid.[1][2] Chemical peels as a class are used for fine lines, acne, acne scars and pigment changes.[2]

A 2014 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology compared a 50% pyruvic acid peel (10 patients) with a 30% salicylic acid peel (10 patients) in people aged 13 to 30 with acne, measuring the amount of sebum secreted on the face.[1] The study is small and no larger randomized trials are listed in the sources reviewed for this article.
Chemical peels of all strengths can cause photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigmentary changes, milia, skin atrophy and scarring, according to a general encyclopedia summary.[2]
Pyruvic acid peels appear in looksmaxxing taxonomies as one of the clinic-based skin-resurfacing options in the hardmaxx category. No substantial forum documentation was found for this article.
